claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
The starting material has an FCC single-phase matrix.
Elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing gas enhances grain-boundary oxidation.
Oxidizing exposure produces continuous, brittle intergranular oxide films, potentially including Al2O3.
Al and possibly other reactive elements diffuse and react preferentially at grain boundaries under oxidizing conditions.
Continuous intergranular oxide films concentrate stress and reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
Oxide-weakened grain boundaries initiate cracks and can precipitate catastrophic failure when applied stress exceeds their reduced strength.
Reducing environments retard or prevent formation of passivating oxide layers.
Retarded or nonuniform passivation in reducing environments permits internal void formation and diffusion-induced damage.
Void formation and diffusion-induced damage in reducing environments compromise cohesion and cause progressive degradation.
Oxidizing exposure will increase intergranular oxide thickness and continuity relative to an inert-atmosphere baseline.
Greater intergranular oxide thickness and continuity will correlate with reduced fracture toughness and earlier sudden crack propagation.
Reducing exposure will produce more internal voiding and less uniform oxide formation than the inert baseline.
Degradation in a reducing atmosphere may proceed more slowly than degradation in an oxidizing atmosphere.
An inert atmosphere at the same temperature will maintain minimal oxide formation.
After inert-atmosphere exposure, ductility and tensile strength are expected to remain at their initial levels.
The proposed behavior applies to exposures above 800 degrees Celsius across strongly oxidizing to strongly reducing atmospheres.
The proposed behavior may not apply at significantly lower temperatures or under sharply different thermal gradients.
Variability in additive-manufacturing-induced microstructures may alter the failure mode.

contradictions.description: Oxide formation is described as a brittle, cohesion-reducing mediator under oxidizing conditions but as protective or passivating under reducing conditions. Different oxide locations or morphologies could reconcile these roles, but that distinction is not explicitly defined.
